newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Mboweni sees rates policy in jobs plan.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Mboweni sees rates policy in jobs plan.

text.p: Monetary policy should be part of the employment strategy South Africa hopes to adopt at a national jobs summit later this year, Labour Minister Tito Mboweni said in an interview.

He told Reuters he hoped the summit, to be led by President Nelson Mandela, would take place in October and would ratify a pre-negotiated package rather than debate employment strategies from scratch.

The labour and trade and industry ministries had drafted a strategy that would be studied soon by a cabinet committee and then submitted to the government's labour and business partners in the National Economic Development and Labour Council (Nedlac) negotiating forum, he said.
Mboweni said estimates of unemployment ranged from 16 percent to more than 30 percent and the total number of jobs available was continuing to decline.
"We can say we are in an unemployment crisis... The problem of unemployment is so huge, so great that it requires a new effort to be put into employment generation.
"We need new mechanisms for the coordination of policies involving government, the private sector, the trade union movement and other stakeholders.
"We need to consider how we manage the financial sector, the interest rate regime, in a manner that does not impact negatively on the whole of the macro economy and the whole of society," he said.

South Africa's economic growth has fallen below the targets set in Finance Minister Trevor Manuel's June 1996 growth, employment and redistribution strategy, known as Gear. What growth has been achieved has been almost entirely jobless.
A Reuter poll of 31 economists in June showed a consensus forecast of 2.1 percent economic growth in 1997, well below the 1997 Gear target of 2.9 percent and last year's 3.1 percent.

Chris Stals, governor of South Africa's independent central Reserve Bank, has come under increasing, though not universal criticism from economists for keeping the key interest rate high at 17 percent since November last year.
Mboweni appeared to echo that concern and criticism levelled also by the Congress of South African Trade Unions when he said:
"We have had the experience where Nedlac discussed a whole range of issues, government put issues on the table and what happens: The following day we hear the Bank has increased interest rates.
"Those interest rates have a massive impact on the macro economy and yet there was no discussion," he said.

The Nedlac council, which includes a financial planning chamber, was set up by President Nelson Mandela's post-apartheid government as a forum for discussion by government, labour and business on key policy issues.
"We are not in any way suggesting that the powers of the Reserve bank should be taken away. Nothing of the sort," said Mboweni.
But he said monetary policy, the exclusive preserve of the Reserve Bank, should be part of the national strategy to create growth and employment.
"It (monetary policy) has to be part of the discussion. I'm sure the Reserve Bank will indicate to us what their views are."
